predecessors.note: The Shang remnant Wu Geng ruled under King Wu's appointment as 'deputy ruler of the eastern lands' (the zhou-dynasty dossier's 1046 gain); the rebellion starts in 1042.

successors.note: 'The Shang domain at Yin was absorbed into Wey, given to Kangshu Feng.' Song, under Weizi Qi, was enfeoffed on 'an ancient Shang cultural center'.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (Cliopatria has no Wu Geng row). The page names Yin as the main base and says King Wu had appointed Wu Geng 'deputy ruler of the eastern lands'; no area or boundary is given. Disc of 80 km round Anyang is the researcher's stand-in; the allies (Pugu and Yan in Shandong, Xu, Ying near the Nanyang Basin) held their own land and are not included.

region.text: Yin, the former Shang capital, Wu Geng's main base ('deputy ruler of the eastern lands')

ledger.note: 1042 BC: Wu Geng rises at Yin. 'In 1042 BC, the second year of the Duke of Zhou's regency, Guanshu and Caishu finally instigated Wu Geng and his followers to rise in rebellion.' The page gives the rebellion as c. 1042-1039 and Yin as his base.

region.text: Yin, the former Shang capital, Wu Geng's main base ('deputy ruler of the eastern lands')

ledger.note: 1041 BC: the rebellion at Yin is crushed. The loyalists 'exterminated the Shang loyalists in the second year of the rebellion', with 'the complete destruction of Yin' and the death of Wu Geng; Guan Shu was executed, Cai Shu fled; the Yin domain went to Wey (Kangshu Feng). Reviewer (ea-01-x, 2026-10-19): confidence 2, not 3: the page gives no BC year for the end ('in the second year of the rebellion'; elsewhere the Duke of Zhou 'defeated the rebels in three years'); 1041 is derived from the 1042 rising, and the zhou-dynasty dossier has its gain at 1039.

wars.name: Rebellion of the Three Guards

zones.text: Yin, the former Shang capital, Wu Geng's main base ('deputy ruler of the eastern lands')
Pugu and Yan, 'both in Shandong', led most Dongyi polities; Xu joined the Huaiyi side

wars.outcome: Zhou victory: Yin destroyed in the second year (1041) and Wu Geng killed; in the third year the royal army attacked the Huai peoples and then defeated Yan; Guan, Yan, Pugu and Cai were dissolved (Cai later revived), Yan's land went to Lu, Pugu's to Qi, Yin to Wey, and Weizi Qi was enfeoffed with Song.
wars.note: The infobox gives c. 1042-1039. A Tsinghua bamboo slip tells a different story in which the Three Guards were killed by the rebels rather than joining them.

certainty.note: Nothing on the page fixes the extent of Wu Geng's domain; Yin and its surroundings only.

sources.title: Rebellion of the Three Guards
sources.note: Rebellion c. 1042-1039 BC; Wu Geng at Yin; allies Pugu, Yan, Xu, Ying; Yin destroyed in the second year; land to Wey, Song, Lu, Qi.

notes: Page opened (1 of 1-2): Rebellion of the Three Guards. Wikidata id left null (unreachable). TYPE rebel (rule 5): the zhou-dynasty dossier (ea-01-a) carries the matching gain at 1039 from 'Wu Geng (Shang remnant) and the eastern peoples'; this dossier ends Wu Geng's own state in 1041 because the page has Yin destroyed 'in the second year of the rebellion' and the third-year campaign hit the Huai peoples and Yan, which are not Wu Geng's land. Cai and Guan (the Zhou-appointed 'Three Guards' guarding Wu Geng) were dissolved and are not dossiers. Pugu and Yan (Shandong), Xu (a Huaiyi state; ea-01-c's Xu dossier) and Ying are allies, not land of this dossier; their fall is in the war zones only. No area on the page, no Cliopatria shape to compare. Related: wey (ea-01-b) was founded 1040 on the Yin domain; song (ea-01-c) at Weizi Qi's enfeoffment; lu and qi took Yan's and Pugu's land. Page silent: Chaoge; the 1039 year of the zhou-dynasty gain is the end of the whole campaign.
